title: The road less travelled part 1
scripture_text: ’’After this, Jesus travelled about from one town and village to another, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom of God. The Twelve were with him, and also some women who had been cured of evil spirits and diseases: Mary (called Magdalene from whom seven demons had come out; Joanna the wife of Chuza, the manager of Herod’s household; Susanna; and many others. These women were helping to support them out of their own means.’’
devotional:
In 1915 the poet Robert Frost published a poem called ‘The road not taken,’ and it may surprise you to know that Frost wrote the poem as a joke for a friend, another poet Edward Thomas. When they went walking together, Thomas was chronically indecisive about which road they ought to take and—in retrospect—often lamented that they should, in fact, have taken the other one. Soon after writing the poem in 1915, Frost griped to Thomas that he had read the poem to an audience of college students and that it had been “taken pretty seriously!’’ Despite the authors original intention, the poem has a serious message. The poem later became a catalyst for a famous book, ‘A Road Less Travelled by M Scott Peck.

The reason I mentioned this is because we want to look at Luke 8:1-3 and as we dig into this passage we are going to discover that it is about a road less travelled, a road of radical discipleship.

Before we look at the passage we need to start by asking the question,

‘What does following Jesus look like in my life?

Could people look at my life and yours, and see that we are people who are zealously following Jesus?

Jesus walked a lonely difficult path. He was out of step with the rest of society, and if we are going to follow him he will lead us along unconventional paths of righteous living. Following Jesus means that we wont be going with the crowds, we won’t be part of the herd. We will have a different agenda which will require a different path.

“The one who follows the crowd will usually go no further from the crowd. The one who walks alone is likely to find himself in places no one has ever been.” — Albert Einstein

Jesus put this way ‘You can enter God’s kingdom through the narrow gate. The highway to hell is broad and its gate is wide for the many who choose that way. But the gateway to life is very narrow and the road is difficult and only a few ever find it.’ Matthew 7:13-14.

The pathway of authentic discipleship is narrow and sparsely populated.

Secondly, these three verses are a microcosm in discipleship. They give us a condensed understanding of what it really means to follow Jesus. They teach or show us in a compact way what discipleship is and how it should shape our lives. These verses in Luke 8:1-3 help us to go through the narrow gate and walk the road that is less travelled.

1 Following Jesus restores our dignity.

Luke tells that among the disciples following Jesus were a number of women, and he mentions three of them, Mary Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Chuza, Herod’s business manager, and Susanna, these and many other women followed Jesus. This was unheard of, for any rabbis to have female disciples was totally unacceptable.

Let me share some of the rabbinic writings about women.

“The female is irrelevant in creation, for she is not more than a parasitic thing taken from him for his utilization to become a special tool for his use as one of his special body parts to be used by him.”

Women were to be shunned in public social contact. Consider the following passage from the Mishna tractate Abot, 1, 5: “Engage not in too much conversation with women.’’

They said this with regard to one’s own wife. How much more does the rule apply to another man’s wife? As long as a man engages in too much conversation with women, he causes evil to himself, for he goes idle from the study of the Torah, so that his end will be that he will inherit gehenna.”

Women were not to be publicly taught the Torah. Consider, however, the following passage from the tractate Sota, 10a: “May the words of Torah be burned, than that they should be handed over to women.” In Sota 21b it is written, “Rabbi Eliezer says: ‘’Whoever teaches his daughter Torah teaches her obscenity.”

This attitude about women’s innate inability to learn the Torah was manifested by having special courts for women in the Second Temple and also in synagogues, where they were separated from men. This was never the practice in the Old Testament. The later practice continues to the present time among Orthodox Jews.

Yet contrary to all the common practices of his day, Jesus had female disciples. Why? Because he saw women as people of dignity. Dignity is the belief that all people hold a special value that's tied solely to their humanity. It has nothing to do with their class, race, gender, religion, abilities, or any other factor other than them being human.
prayer: Father as men we thank you for the ladies you have brought into our lives may we treat them as Jesus would.
